paragraphs.text: Psalmus totus luctuosus, a doleful ditty, beginning and ending with complaints; and therefore sung in the primitive times, among other penitential psalms, as the public confession of persons excommunicated.
A musical instrument sounding heavily as a shaulm doth, and therefore called infirmity, for humbling, or for antiphenies. A fit title.

i.e. The instruction of Heman, who was a very wise man, 1Ki 4:31, descended of Zerah, the son of Judah, 1Ch 2:4, and thence called the Ezrahite, brother to Ethan, who penned the next psalm, 1Ch 2:6. Nobile par fratrum.

This is the only one expression of his faith found in this whole psalm, and it nmst be understood that he thus believed and prayed, as here, Psa 88:2, when he was at worst, and most despairingly complained.
paragraphs.anchor: O Lord God of my salvation

paragraphs.text: Though in such a state as they were, Act 27:20, when neither sun nor star appeared, yet he cast anchor, and prayed still for day.
paragraphs.anchor: I have cried day and night unto thee

paragraphs.text: He did not cast out brutish and wild complaints and moans in misery, as it is natural for people to do, but poured forth his soul into God’s blessed bosom, and now prayeth an answer.
paragraphs.anchor: Let my prayer come before thee

paragraphs.text: Hypotyposis hominis luctuosissime affecti. Here we have the lively picture of a man under bitter affliction. Extraordinary wise he was, and extraordinary troubles he had. None out of hell suffer more than God’s dearest children. This good man felt himself in the suburbs of hell, as it were.
paragraphs.anchor: For my soul is full of trouble

paragraphs.text: Or, unto hell. The same word signifieth both, because death is hell’s harbinger, and would be so to the elect, but for Christ.
paragraphs.anchor: And my life draweth nigh unto the grave

paragraphs.text: I am looked upon as irrecoverable, given up for desperate. Conclamatum est.
A man no man; weak as water, ακιας αναρ ανθρωπος.
paragraphs.anchor: I am as a man that hath no strength

paragraphs.text: Free of that company, one of the many among the manes, or ghosts; a free denizen of that society of that moiety of mankind that are dead. Yea, I am mortuorum minimus, as R. Jonah rendereth it, according to the Arabic, A mundo manumissus.
That are thrown on heaps into a pit, as after a field fought (R. David).
paragraphs.anchor: Like the slain that lie in the grave

paragraphs.text: As to this present world, and as it may seem to others, with whom out of sight out of mind; dead folk are soon forgotten. Varro thinks Lethum, death, hath its name απο την ληθης, from forgetfulness; because they which have now forgotten all the world should soon be forgotten of the world.
Thy providence over them in matters belonging to life is at an end.
paragraphs.anchor: And they are cut off from thine hand

paragraphs.text: In cisterna infimorum, in the deepest dungeon, in lutoso lacu, such as Jeremiah was cast into, Jer 37:15-16
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit

paragraphs.text: In voraginibus, out of which none escapes, nothing can be buoyed up, as they call it.
So it did upon David, Psa 32:3, but especially upon the Son of David, the Lord Christ, of whose sufferings these were but types, or as chips of his cross.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy wrath lieth hard upon me

paragraphs.text: But all this while it is thy doing, and that carrieth comfort in it.
paragraphs.anchor: And thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves

paragraphs.text: Job and David complain of the like misery. Optimum solatium sodalitium; but woe to him that is alone.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast put away mine acquaintance, &c.

paragraphs.text: Miserably inclaved in this forlorn comfortless condition, a perpetual prisoner.

Which he would not have done if he had cast away his confidence; for "how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?" Rom 10:14. The saints, when they want the sun, yet they have the daystar in their hearts.
paragraphs.anchor: Lord, I have called daily upon thee

paragraphs.text: Wilt thou delay to deliver me till I am dead, and then raise me again by a miracle, that I may praise thee? But he should have considered that God neither needeth our poor praises nor can his help ever come too late.
paragraphs.anchor: Wilt thou show wonders to the dead?

paragraphs.text: Heb. the giants, that is, those that are swallowed up of death, as the giants were of the deluge.
The same again, and Psa 88:12 a third time, pro more dolentium. See Psa 6:5; Psa 30:9.
So the state and place of the dead is called; and why: {See Trapp on "Psa 88:5"}
Oh, condescend to thy poor crying creature in extremity.
paragraphs.anchor: But unto thee have I cried

paragraphs.text: {See Trapp on "Psa 5:3"}

Luther saith of himself, that after his conversion he lay three days in desperation. And afterwards, he sometimes suffered such desertions, ut nec calor, nec sanguis, nec sensus, nec vex, superesset, saith an eyewitness (Just. Jon. Ep. ad Melan.).

He was brought up in the school of temptations, and kept in this form from his youth. He was put soon to it, and so deep lessons had he set him, that he had like to have lost his wits. I am distracted, saith he, I am held upon the wheel.
As rivers of brimstone.
Multis excisionibus ideoque duplicatur Tau.
As the water compasseth the earth like a girdle.
See Psa 88:8, and mark how mournfully he concludeth; as doth also the Church, Lam 5:22.
